text.content: This chapter covers close-combat armaments, from vibroblades and force pikes to the iconic lightsaber — its components, construction, and modification. Ranged weapons and explosives are detailed in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.gxAN3kXd5U4q1H3c]{Chapter 11}.

While blasters dominate many battlefields, a well-placed blade or brutal blow can be just as decisive. These weapons utilize everything from raw strength to ultrasonic vibrations to gain an edge in close quarters.

Terms

Reach determines how far a character can strike with a melee weapon or unarmed attack. It is measured in yards, corresponding to hex distances on a tactical map.

For example, a punch or knife has Reach C (Close), a sword usually has Reach 1, and a spear has Reach 2 or more.

Durability (DUR) represents the overall durability of a weapon, each weapon has a set DUR value.

  • Any time a weapon is the direct target of an attack or sustains a “Hard Hit” (an attack roll that exceeds the defender’s active defense by a significant margin, e.g., 5+), the attack damage is compared to the weapon type’s DUR
  • Subtract the weapon's Dur from the basic penetrating damage rolled against it and read the remainder on @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}'s Weapon Damage Thresholds: 1 to 10 points drops it to Damaged and shaves 1 off its Dur until repaired; 11 to 19 leaves it Broken; 20 or more destroys it outright if the blow came from a cutting weapon, a lightsaber or a shaped charge. @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7} is the authority here -- a single heavy blow can ruin a weapon, and it does not take three of them.
  • The transition happens automatically when the stress threshold is breached.
  • Fine: Optimal condition.
  • Damaged: The item has taken structural stress. Its Malfunction range widens -- see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7} -- and its Dur is 1 lower until repaired.
  • Broken: Inoperable. The weapon cannot strike or parry until it is overhauled at a workshop.
  • Destroyed: Irreparable scrap. It can only be broken down for parts.
  • If an item is Broken or Destroyed, it can no longer be repaired in the field - it must be brought to a workshop or broken down for parts.
  • Characters can use Armoury or Mechanic skill (time required: 10 minutes per item) to “clean” a Damaged item. If they succeed by 3+, restore it to Fine.

Key Reach Mechanics

  • Reach C (Close Combat): Targets adjacent to your hex. This is used for all unarmed attacks, grapples, and very short weapons. If a combatant gets inside a longer weapon’s reach, that weapon takes a penalty to parry and attack.
  • Reach 1: Attacks targets 1 yard away (the next hex over on a grid).
  • Variable Reach: Many weapons list options like “C,1” (can attack Close or 1 yard away). Others like “1,2” require a Ready maneuver to change the weapon’s grip or stance between Close and Extended.
  • Longer Reaches (Reach 2+): Weapons like polearms and spears allow attacking foes before they can step into melee range. However, you must be careful: if a foe closes the gap, they can bypass your weapon’s advantage.

Modifiers and Tactics

  • Size Modifier (SM): Taller or massive characters/creatures naturally have a larger Reach. For every point your Size Modifier is above 0, your reach generally increases by 1 yard.
  • The “Wait” Maneuver: If an opponent with a shorter reach attempts to step into your Reach 2 or 3 zone, you can declare a Wait maneuver to attack them before their turn happens. This is an essential tactic for polearm or spear users keeping aggressors at bay.
  • Committed and All-Out Attacks: You can temporarily increase your reach by 1 yard using specific maneuvers like Committed Attack (Long) or All-Out Attack (Long), though doing so usually decreases your defensive capabilities.

Parry is an Active Defense used to deflect a melee attack using a weapon, or your bare hands.

Parry Formula

To calculate your base Parry score, use the following formula:

Parry = 3 + (Melee Skill Level / 2 )

  • Round Down: Always drop any fractions.
  • For example, a Broadsword skill of 13 gives a Parry of 3 + 6 = 9.
  • Default (No Skill): If you have no training in a weapon or unarmed skill, you use your Dexterity attribute: 3 + (DX / 2).

Standard Modifiers

  • Retreating (+3): You can step backward one yard relative to your attacker as part of your defense, gaining a +3 bonus to fencing weapons (like rapiers) or a +1 bonus to all other parries.
  • Off-Hand Parry (-1): Parrying with a weapon in your off-hand incurs a -1 penalty, matching the -4 to hit and -1 to parry given under Dual Wielding Weapons in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}. Ambidexterity removes both; so does a lightsaber form incorporating Jar’Kai (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.BUSu7dFLs9IzOvPY]{Chapter 9}).
  • Shield DB: If you are carrying a shield, its Defense Bonus (DB) is added directly to your Parry roll.

Multiple Parries

You can parry more than once per combat turn, but subsequent attempts become increasingly difficult:

  • Standard Weapons: Each successive parry with the same weapon suffers a cumulative -4 penalty (-4 for the second, -8 for the third, etc.).
  • Fencing Weapons & Weapon Masters: The cumulative penalty is reduced to a cumulative -2 per extra parry.
  • Two Weapons: If you dual-wield, you can parry once with each weapon on the same turn before tracking cumulative penalties on a per-weapon basis.

Critical Weapon Properties

  • Unbalanced Weapons (“U”): Weapons with a “U” next to their parry stat (like many heavy axes, maces, or flails) cannot attack and parry in the same turn, unless the wielder possesses 1.5× the weapon’s required ST — see Unbalanced Weapons under Melee Combat Notes for the full rule.
  • If you swing it, you cannot use it to parry until your next turn.
  • Parrying Heavy Weapons: If you parry a weapon that weighs more than three times your own weapon’s weight, your weapon risks breaking.

Unarmed Parrying

  • Parrying Weapons Barehanded: If you use Brawling or default DX to parry a weapon attack, you take a -3 penalty.
  • Karate and Judo skills completely bypass this penalty.
  • Weapon vs. Unarmed: If you successfully parry an unarmed attack (like a punch or kick) using a weapon, you may instantly roll against your weapon skill to damage the attacker’s striking limb automatically.

ST (Strength) stat for a weapon determines the minimum Strength required to use it without penalties.

For muscle-powered weapons (like swords or bows), it also serves as the baseline for calculating damage (Thrust or Swing).

Key ST Mechanics

  • Minimum ST Requirement: If your character’s ST is lower than a weapon’s listed minimum ST, whether melee or ranged, you suffer a -1 skill penalty for every point you are short.
  • Unbalanced Weapons: Melee weapons whose Parry stat carries a U (e.g., Parry -1U) cannot be used to Parry in the same turn you Attack unless you possess 1.5× the required ST. Do not confuse this with the dagger on a weapon's ST, which marks it two-handed -- the two markers are independent, and a weapon may carry either, both, or neither.
  • Damage Scaling: Your Thrust (thr) and Swing (sw) dice increase with your ST score.
  • You check your ST value against the GURPS Strength Table, find your base damage, and apply the weapon’s modifier (e.g., sw+2).
  • High ST Perks: If your ST is 1.5× to 2× higher than a weapon’s requirement, you gain combat advantages, such as ignoring “unready” requirements on heavy weapons like two-handed axes.
  • One-Handing a Two-Handed Weapon: You may wield a two-handed (†) weapon in one hand at -2 to hit, or -4 if it is Unbalanced (U). One-handed it handles as Unbalanced -- no attacking and parrying in the same turn until you have 1.5× its Min ST -- and the to-hit penalty is halved at 1.5× Min ST and removed at 2×, the same band as the perk above. It stacks with the Minimum ST shortfall and, if the weapon is in your off hand, with the off-hand penalties (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). A weapon marked ‡ is the exception: it is built for one- or two-handed use and takes no one-handing penalty.
  • Can Become Unready (◊): A weapon marked ◊ is thrown off balance by its own swing: after you attack with it, it is unready, and you must take a Ready maneuver to re-balance it (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}) before you can attack with it again. Strength cancels this -- at 1.5× the weapon’s Min ST you ignore the unready entirely (see High ST Perks, above).

Special Rules Glossary

  • Lightsaber Resistant: The weapon is made of a rare material (like Beskar, Phrik, or Cortosis) or has a unique energy field.
  • It can Parry a lightsaber without being destroyed.
  • This does not protect the wielder, only the weapon itself.
  • **Reach (*):** A weapon with an asterisked Reach (e.g., 2, 3*) becomes unready after an attack at that maximum distance and requires a Ready maneuver before it can be used to attack or parry again.
  • Shock Effect: Delivers a painful jolt of electricity.
  • On a successful hit, the target takes both Endurance (EP) and a small amount of Burning (burn) damage.
  • Target must make a HT roll to avoid being Stunned, at a penalty equal to the amount of burning damage taken.
  • Stun Effect: Designed for non-lethal takedowns.
  • On a successful hit, the user can choose to deal no normal damage and instead deliver a stun charge.
  • The target takes 3d Endurance (EP) damage and must make a HT-5 roll to avoid being physically Stunned for 1d seconds.
  • Unbalanced (U): The weapon is poorly balanced for defense.
  • It gives a penalty to Parry attempts. A Parry of +0U is simply
  • Unbalanced and gives no bonus or penalty to Parry, but cannot benefit from effects that improve parries.

Powered Melee Weapons

Many weapons in this armory are powered by internal, rechargeable energy cells. When their charge is depleted, they can still be used as simple, unpowered clubs or blades, losing any bonus damage, armor divisors, or elemental effects.

  • Charge Capacity: Indicated in the “Charges” column for each weapon. Unpowered weapons are marked “N/A”.
  • Recharging: A depleted weapon can be fully recharged in 10 minutes when connected to a standard power source (such as a power socket on a starship or a portable generator).

Shock Weapons (Discharge-Based)

Designed to incapacitate foes through electrical discharge or concussive force, these weapons expend power instantly upon impact.

  • Powered Strike (Shock): Costs 1 charge per successful hit.
  • The weapon deals its normal crushing damage plus a follow-up “Shock” effect, which inflicts both Endurance (EP) and a small amount of Burning (burn) damage.
  • A target taking any burn damage from the shock must make a HT roll, at a penalty equal to the burn damage taken, or be physically Stunned.
  • Stun Discharge: A focused, non-lethal attack that costs 2 charges. This powerful discharge replaces the weapon’s normal damage. The target takes 3d Endurance (EP) and must make a HT-5 roll to avoid being physically Stunned for 1d seconds.

Vibro & Elemental Weapons (Duration-Based)

Weapons utilizing ultrasonic vibration (Vibroblades) or elemental fields (Echani, Baragwin) must remain continuously active during a fight to impart their special effects.

  • Activation: Igniting the ultrasonic generator or energy field requires a Ready maneuver (or a Free Action, if modified with a specific trigger).
  • Power Consumption: The weapon consumes 1 charge per minute of continuous activation.

Modular Components & Base Materials

A character wishing to build, modify, or break down a weapon must interact with its discrete components. Each structural component lists its Volume in cubic feet (ft^3).

To calculate the final weight and cost of a structural component, use the following formulas based on the chosen material:

  • Weight = Volume x Density (Density is lbs/ft^3)
  • Cost = Weight x Cost Per lb. (Round up to the next whole Credit)

Final Component Dur = Base Dur Mod x Material Dur Multiplier

(Round normally to the nearest whole number).

The total weight, cost and Parry of a weapon are the sum of its parts. For Parry, add the Parry Mod of each structural component -- Grip, Head, Guard -- and read the total off the weapon's line; utility items and power units contribute nothing, since a vibro-generator does not change how a blade handles. A component marked U is unbalanced, and any weapon built with one is itself unbalanced and cannot attack and parry in the same turn unless the wielder has 1.5× the weapon’s required ST. Durability works the same way but is computed per part first: each structural component's Base Dur Mod is multiplied by its own material's Dur Multiplier and rounded, and those results are then added.

  • The market price for components is the base material cost × 2 for Phase 1, Armoury (Melee Weapons) or Smith (both IQ/Average) -- round the material value up to the next whole credit first, then multiply.
  • Lightsaber handgrip components are the exception on both counts: they need Lightsaber Construction (IQ/Hard), so theirs is × 3, and their rounding comes last -- ceil(material value × 3), a single ceiling on the finished price.
  • Two Rounding Orders: The two orders are not interchangeable and they are not close: measured against this chapter's own printed figures, melee rounds first on 75 of 75 components and the lightsaber order rounds last on 20 of 20 Handgrip parts. They agree by coincidence on a handful of parts, so a component priced in the wrong order can still look right -- check a part whose material value has a fraction, never one that lands whole.
  • Weight Basis: In both families the material value is figured from the unrounded weight; printed weights are rounded to two decimals for display and are not what the price derives from.
  • @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.gxAN3kXd5U4q1H3c]{Chapter 11} Differs: @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.gxAN3kXd5U4q1H3c]{Chapter 11} does not work this way: it truncates component weight to two decimals and prices from the truncated figure, and says so. The two chapters open with the same formula line and it does not mean the same thing in both -- take the convention from the chapter you are in, never from the sentence.
  • The market price for an assembled weapon is its Base Cost multiplied by every phase its construction requires, one at a time -- see Crafting Phases under Crafting Melee Weapons. A plain blade takes one use beyond its components: ×2 for Phase 2, Armoury (Melee Weapons) at IQ/Average. A powered weapon takes that same ×2, then a further ×3 for Phase 3, Armstech (weapon’s specialty) at IQ/Hard.
  • Market prices can be inflated or deflated based on location.

Base Materials & Suitability

Materials dictate the mass and cost of the weapon, as well as distinct combat effects.

  • Main Suitability: The material can be milled and forged to create the core structure of a Grip, Head, or Guard.
  • Wrap/Coating Suitability: The material can be applied over a component. Wraps (Grips) add 0.0001 ft³ to the weapon’s volume. Coatings/Weaves (Blades/Guards) add 0.0002 ft³ to the weapon’s volume.

Crafting Melee Weapons

Crafting Phases: A melee weapon takes two phases, and a powered one takes three (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Construction Markup).

  • Phase 1 is Component Forging -- shaping each Hilt, Grip, Head and Guard from raw stock -- and needs Armoury (Melee Weapons) or Smith, both IQ/Average, so it multiplies by ×2; that markup is already in each component's listed price.
  • Phase 2 is Hardware Assembly, joining those components into a balanced weapon, and also needs Armoury (Melee Weapons), IQ/Average, so it multiplies the Base Cost by ×2.
  • Phase 3 applies only to a weapon carrying a Power Cell and an active emitter: Power Unit Integration needs Armstech (weapon’s specialty), IQ/Hard, so it multiplies the running total by ×3.

Applying the Phases: Apply them in order. A plain blade stops after Phase 2; a vibro or shock weapon carries on through Phase 3. Lightsabers are handled separately below, under Crafting Internal Components and Example Lightsaber Hilts.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- whether it appears in this chapter’s tables or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy the plan for a catalog item, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original through the Design Phase. Owning or knowing of an item is not knowing how to make one. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every Crafting Phase roll below.

Crafting a custom modular weapon requires both metallurgical skill and, for powered variants, precise electronic calibration.

Pricing Note: All component and finished-item prices below follow the Construction Markup formula defined in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): each construction step is marked up by the tier of the skill that step needs -- ×1.5 Easy, ×2 Average, ×3 Hard, ×4 Very Hard. See Markup Tier, above, for which skill applies to which step in this chapter.

Skills Required

  • Physical & Structural Components: Armoury (Melee Weapons) or Smith to forge, shape, and balance the Hilt/Grip, Head, and Guard based on their structural volume.
  • Powered & Energy Components: Armstech (weapon’s specialty) or Armoury (Melee Weapons) combined with Electronics Repair (Powered Melee) to seamlessly integrate vibro-generators, power cells, and shock emitters.
  • Software Initialization (Silicon): Weapons constructed with Silicon components (vibro-generators, shock emitters) require a Computer Programming or Electronics Operation roll after assembly to tune the frequencies and prevent the weapon from tearing itself apart.
  • Default appearance. A weapon with no finish specified looks like the material it is made of: Durasteel dull gunmetal gray; Plasteel off-white; Bronzium warm brown-gold; Cortosis matte black, light-drinking; Phrik dark silver-blue; Beskar bright polished silver; Mullinine pale blue-white; Reflec near-black with an oily shimmer; Electrum warm pale gold; Aurodium rich yellow gold; Plastoid bone white; Synth-Leather mid-brown; Fibercord drab gray; Standard Timber plain light brown; Brylark Wood dense black-brown; Greel Wood streaked purple-gray; Japor Ivory creamy off-white; Wroshyr Wood deep red-brown grain; Scrap Metal rusted and pitted; Scrap Cloth faded and mismatched. A weapon built from several materials shows its Base component's finish unless the player says otherwise.
  • Coloring: Finish is free and changes nothing — no weight, no cost, no Damage, Parry, Reach or Dur. A crafter working at a dedicated workshop or better (the +0 or +2 Workspace tier — see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}’s Shared Skills & Workspace for the shared scale) simply declares the color, pattern or finish of anything they build, with no roll and no extra time; the Plastoid and Synth-Leather grip wraps in the tables below are listed at their plain @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} rates for this reason, coloured or not. Improvised/Field Tools and a Basic Toolkit can produce the weapon but not finish it, and it comes out the default shade of its material. The same applies to refinishing a weapon already made.
  • Blade color is not a finish. A lightsaber's blade takes its color from its Primary Focusing Crystal, not from any paint or plating, and it cannot be changed at a workbench — only by swapping the crystal (see Lightsaber Crystals below). The hilt is ordinary hardware and may be finished freely like any other weapon.

Assembly Sequence

Phase 1: Component Forging (Hardware)

The crafter procures the base materials (Durasteel, Bronzium, Cortosis, Silicon, etc.) calculating the necessary amount via the component’s volume formula (Weight = Volume Density).

  • Time Required: 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the final calculated weight.
  • The Roll: A single skill check per component.
  • Success: The component is forged perfectly to spec.
  • Failure: The material warps. 50% of the raw material mass is lost as unrecoverable scrap; the rest can be melted down and tried again.
  • Critical Failure: 100% of the raw material is destroyed. Crafter takes 1d-3 burning/crushing damage from a forge accident.

Phase 2: Hardware Assembly

Joining the Grips, Heads, and Guards into a balanced weapon.

  • Time Required: 2 hours.
  • The Roll: Armoury (Melee Weapons).
  • Success: The weapon is perfectly balanced.
  • Failure: The weapon is off-balance, suffering a -1 penalty to Parry until disassembled and re-seated.

Phase 3: Power Unit Integration (Electronics)

If the weapon requires a Power Cell and an active emitter (Vibro/Shock).

  • Time Required: 1 hour of tuning and frequency calibration.
  • The Roll: Armstech (weapon’s specialty) or Electronics Repair (Powered Melee).
  • Success: The frequency matches the blade. The weapon functions perfectly.
  • Failure: The generator misaligns. No parts are wasted, but the crafter must spend another hour debugging.
  • Critical Failure: Hidden flaw. The weapon appears to function but will suffer a critical breakage or power overload on its first strike in combat.
  • Workspace Modifiers: Improvised/Field Tools -5, Basic Toolkit -2, Dedicated Workshop/Lab +0, Advanced Research Facility +2 -- the four-tier scale from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (see The Four Tiers), named for this trade. A lightsaber cannot be built below the +0 tier at all: the crystal alignment will not hold on a camp bench.
  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Installing/Swapping Components

Swapping a Grip, Head, Guard, or Power Unit on a fully assembled weapon requires breaking the structural seals and realigning the balance. The removed component comes out intact, retaining its own established Base/Market Cost value for reuse or resale.

  • Base Time: 30 minutes per component swapped.
  • Skill Required: Armoury (Melee Weapons) for structural parts; Armstech (weapon’s specialty) for Power Units.
  • Failure: The new part is improperly mounted. The weapon is non-functional until another 30 minutes are spent realigning it.

Deconstructing Melee Weapons

While Salvaging is a fast method for reducing a weapon down to its generic raw materials (e.g., pounds of Durasteel, Cortosis, or Diatium) for smelting or a quick payout, Deconstruction is the meticulous process of breaking a weapon down to preserve its discrete, fully functional modular components. This is ideal for mechanics looking to strip a pristine High-Frequency Vibro-Generator, a Cortosis Weave Grip, or an intact Beskar Blade from a captured weapon to install on their own custom hilt or chassis.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction is also the moment to record a Blueprint of the weapon (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll, made during the teardown. Salvaging never yields one.

Phase 1: Meticulous Disassembly (Hardware)

  • Skills: Armoury (Melee Weapons) for standard weapons. Lightsaber Construction is required for lightsabers specifically -- Armoury does not apply to them.
  • Time: 30 minutes of labor per pound of the weapon’s scaled weight (twice as long as salvaging).
  • Success: Safely extracts one intact, reusable structural component or modification of the crafter's choice (e.g., the Blade/Head, the Hilt/Grip, the Power Unit, or a specific Edge/Accent Mod), retaining its established Base/Market Cost value from the component breakdown above for reuse in a new build. For every 2 points of Margin of Success, one additional intact component may be safely extracted. Anything not extracted intact comes back as raw material separated by type, at 75% of its weight -- 90% on a critical success.
  • Critical Success: Flawless teardown. Every discrete modular component and installed modification making up the weapon is extracted fully intact and ready for immediate reassembly.
  • Failure: A stripped threading, snapped ultrasonic channel, or clumsy pry-bar ruins the attempt. The targeted component is warped and rendered non-functional. The weapon is destroyed, yielding only 25% of its base raw material weight in scrap.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic mishandling of the weapon's energy gates, power cell, or vibration generator causes a violent backlash. All components are completely destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 damage from an electrical shock or sudden spring release.

Phase 2: Component Calibration & Wiping (Electronics/Power) Any extracted component that natively requires a power source or complex electronics (such as Vibration Generators, Stun Modulators, Shock Emitters, or Power Cells -- see the Utility Item table above) retains its previous hardware registry, security protocols, and energy alignment. It must be carefully scrubbed and recalibrated before it can successfully "handshake" with a new weapon.

  • Skills: Electronics Repair (Powered Melee) or Computer Programming (for biometric/security locks).
  • Time: 30 minutes of calibration or data-wiping per electronic/powered component extracted.
  • Success: The component's power matrix is stabilized and any firmware is wiped clean, restoring it to a factory-default state ready for installation into a new build.
  • Failure: The component's anti-tamper software triggers, or the energy gates temporarily lock up. The physical component is unharmed, but it cannot be installed until a dedicated repair or slicing attempt (requires an hour and an Electronics Repair or Computer Programming roll at -2) bypasses the lock.
  • Critical Failure: The recalibration accidentally cascades into the hardware's physical logic gates or overloads the miniature power matrix, permanently "bricking" the powered component. The item is rendered completely useless.

Salvaging Melee Weapons

Breaking down captured or broken melee weapons allows characters to reclaim valuable raw materials (by weight based on volume), silicon components, and delicate emitters.

Phase 1: Stripping the Weapon

Breaking the Head, Grip, Guard and Power Units down for material rather than for reuse -- fast work, and nothing comes out fit to refit. A crafter who wants the parts intact should Deconstruct instead.

  • Skill Required: Armoury (Melee Weapons) for standard weapons; Armstech (weapon’s specialty) where a Power Unit has to come out live. Lightsabers do not use this section -- see Salvaging, below, and @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}'s Lightsaber Construction: every part of a lightsaber falls under that skill, and Armoury does not apply to them.
  • Time Required: 15 minutes of labor per pound of the weapon.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check for the weapon.
  • Success: The weapon is stripped, recovering 50% of its original raw material weight. A Critical Success recovers 75% and preserves one intact, reusable component or treatment of the salvager's choice.
  • Failure: The teardown is clumsy -- threading strips, housings crush, and the yield is 0.
  • Critical Failure: A power cell punctures or a vibration generator violently misaligns. The component is destroyed entirely, and the salvager takes 1d-3 damage.

Phase 2: Material Breakdown (Smelting)

Reducing an intact component back into its raw base materials -- a part pulled cleanly by Deconstruction, a spare from the shelf, or a treatment stripped off a blade. This is not part of stripping a whole weapon, which Phase 1 already covers: it is melting down something that is currently whole, which is why the yield is better than a teardown's.

  • Skill Required: Scrounging or Machinist.
  • Time Required: 30 minutes per component.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check.
  • Success: Recovers 75% of the component’s original raw material weight.

A lightsaber is more than just a weapon; it is a deeply personal extension of the user’s will, which they channel through it. Energy constantly flows through the lightsaber’s kyber crystal, and when fighting with one, the user is not swinging a simple blade, as much as directing a heavy current of power. Each lightsaber is usually customized to the user’s unique connection to the Force and combat style.

While the heart of the lightsaber is its focusing crystal, several other key components can be chosen and upgraded to enhance its performance. This guide expands upon the lightsaber creation rules, offering a system for upgradeable parts, including lenses, emitter matrices, and energy cells.

Notes:

  • Lightsabers draw power from an internal power cell.
  • Lightsabers are usually constructed by the user, or taken off a defeated Lightsaber wielder. Purchasing a Lightsaber is generally only possible on the black market and they are usually difficult to acquire.
  • Lightsaber hilts have a base Dur of 10 and must be directly targeted at a -5 penalty.

The Core Parts of a Lightsaber

As detailed in the provided holocron data, the construction of a lightsaber is a rite of passage for many Force-users, requiring both technical skill and a deep connection to the Force. The essential components remain:

  • Handgrip: The chassis of the weapon, housing all other components. This part is customized with different types of hilt components, and materials to build those components with.
  • Power Cell: The source of the lightsaber’s energy.
  • Emitter Matrix: Projects the energy from the crystal into a coherent blade.
  • Lens Assembly: Focuses the energy from the crystal.
  • Primary Focusing Crystal: The heart of the lightsaber, determining its primary colors, and characteristics.
  • Secondary Focusing Crystal/ Power Crystal: Optional, determines the lightsabers additional characteristics.

Lightsaber Components

Beyond basic construction, the performance of a lightsaber is entirely determined by its physical chassis and internal components. This bottom-up system allows for a massive degree of customization. The overall combat skill required to wield the weapon is dictated by its Base/Pommel and Sleeve, while the damage and special effects are dictated by the Emitter and Crystals.

A standard, single-bladed lightsaber requires one of each of the following: Emitter, Switch, Sleeve, Pommel, Power Cell, Lens, Emitter Matrix, and Kyber Crystal. Secondary Power Crystals are optional.

Applicable Lightsaber Combat (Class Type) skill is determined by the combined classes of the Handgrip.

  • Class Type = Emitter Class + Sleeve Class + Base Class
  • In the case of multiple classes which share the same name, add only 1 to the Class Type (e.g.,Standard emitter + Standard Sleeve + Pike Pommel would be Lightsaber Combat (Standard Pike)).
  • For dual-bladed builds, the Class Type simply lists all unique Class names across both sides in structural order (Emitter(s) > Sleeve(s) > Base).

Examples

  • Lightwhip + Curved + Pike = Lightsaber Combat (Lightwhip Curved Pike)
  • Standard + Standard + Standard = Lightsaber Combat (Standard)
  • Crossguard + Standard + Jar’Kai-Saberstaff + Crossguard + Standard + Jar’Kai-Saberstaff = Lightsaber Combat (Crossguard Standard Jar’Kai-Saberstaff)
  • Lightwhip + Curved + Saberstaff + Standard + Shoto + Saberstaff = Lightsaber Combat (Lightwhip Standard Curved Shoto Saberstaff)

If a character lacks the applicable Lightsaber Combat (Class Type) skill for the weapon they are wielding, they may use any other Lightsaber Combat (Class Type) skill they know at -1. This -1 replaces the -2 that @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3} applies between specialties of the same skill; it is the same flat -1 generalist convention used by Guns (Any).

Because the system is modular, resolving unusual builds is a matter of combining the traits of the chosen parts.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. (Assembling the finished lightsaber from its parts is the exception -- see Lightsaber Assembly under Constructing a Lightsaber, below.)

Crafting the outer chassis components requires milling, shaping, and treating the raw metals and materials before they can be assembled into a functional handgrip. Step 1: Material Procurement and Calculation The crafter must acquire the raw materials (e.g., Durasteel, Electrum, Beskar). The required weight and value of the raw material are calculated using the specific component’s volume (e.g., 0.0008 ft³ for a Standard Sleeve) multiplied by the material’s density and cost per pound.

Step 2: Milling and Shaping Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. Time Required: 2 to 4 hours per component, depending on material rarity and hardness (e.g., Phrik or Beskar takes twice as long). The Roll: Make a single skill check to properly forge and thread the individual piece.

  • Critical Success / Success: The component is forged perfectly to spec. It is structurally sound, perfectly weighted, and ready for future assembly.
  • Standard Failure: The material warps or the threading is stripped during the milling process. The component is useless. You lose 50% of the raw material mass as unrecoverable shavings; the rest can be melted down and tried again.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic error ruins the temper of the metal or triggers a forge accident. 100% of the raw material is destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy or crushing damage from a tool slip or localized flash-melt.

Applies to breaking down uninstalled Emitters, Sleeves, Switches, and Pommels into raw scrap metal.

Step 1: Breakdown and Smelting Skill Check Required: Scrounging or Machinist. Time Required: 30 minutes per component. The Roll: Make a single skill check to separate and refine the useful metals from the scrap.

  • Standard Failure: The breakdown is sloppy, mixing alloys or burning off valuable metals. The salvager recovers only 25% of the component’s raw material weight.
  • Critical Failure: The material is completely ruined, oxidized, or slagged beyond use. Yields 0% recoverable materials.

Crafting Internal Components

Applies to Power Cells, Lens Assemblies, and Emitter Matrices.

Fabricating the delicate internal electronics and optical arrays requires precise micro-soldering and chemical alignment.

Step 1: Material Procurement The crafter must gather the exact base materials required for the specific component (e.g., 0.05 lbs of Clari-crystalline and 0.05 lbs of Cortosis for a Firkrann Lens, or Diatium and Aurodium for a Corusca Gem Power Cell).

Step 2: Micro-Fabrication Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. Time Required: 1d hours per component. The Roll: Make a single skill check to fuse the base materials, align the optics, or charge the cells.

  • Critical Success / Success: The internal component is flawlessly created. Diatium cells hold their maximum charge, lenses are perfectly clear, and matrices are properly insulated. The component is ready for future integration.
  • Standard Failure: A micro-fracture forms in the clari-crystalline, or the diatium fails to hold a charge. The component does not function. No base materials are permanently destroyed, but the crafter must spend 1 additional hour re-cutting or re-soldering the materials and attempt a new roll.
  • Critical Failure: The materials violently reject the fabrication process. The volatile base materials (such as Diatium or unstable crystals) fuse and short out. 100% of the base materials are destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy damage from an immediate chemical or electrical flash.

Salvaging Internal Components

Applies to breaking down uninstalled Power Cells, Lenses, and Emitter Matrices into their base raw materials.

If an individual possesses a standalone internal component and wishes to break it down to extract its valuable base materials (e.g., trying to safely extract the Phrik from a Phond Cell or the Electrum from a Velmorite Matrix) without integrating it into a lightsaber.

Step 1: Chemical and Electronic Separation Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction -- these are lightsaber internals, and the skill that fabricates them is the skill that takes them apart. A salvager without it may attempt Electronics Repair (Powered Melee) or Armoury (Melee Weapons) at a -3 penalty, working blind against the microscopic fusing of the parts. Time Required: 1 hour per component. The Roll: Make a single skill check to carefully de-solder, uncouple, and separate the raw base materials.

  • Critical Success / Success: The delicate separation is a success. The salvager safely extracts the discrete base materials (e.g., separating the Clari-crystalline from the Aurodium in a Dragite Lens), preserving 75% of their original base material weight for future use.
  • Standard Failure: The salvager’s tools slip. The lens shatters, or the matrix circuit board snaps. The component is ruined as junk, yielding absolutely zero recoverable base materials.
  • Critical Failure: A residual charge in the uninstalled module triggers a violent discharge during separation. All base materials are completely destroyed, and the salvager takes 1d-3 energy damage from the resulting micro-plasma burst.

Example Lightsaber Hilts

Market Cost = Base Cost × 3. Base Cost is the sum of every already-marked-up Handgrip component (above), plus the Power Cell, Lens, Matrix, and Kyber Crystal at their own established prices (these are Already-Finished Components, not re-marked-up here). Mark up and round each Handgrip component separately -- component price = ceil(component weight × CR/lb × 3) -- then add them together; do not pool the raw values and round once at the end, which gives a different figure on some builds. A weapon with two blades carries two of every internal as well as two of each doubled Handgrip part. The final ×3 represents the Lightsaber Construction (IQ/Hard) roll that assembles everything into a working weapon -- the same Hard-difficulty markup tier as the components themselves.

Handgrip prices are printed, not recomputed. Each Emitter, Sleeve, Switch and Base/Pommel table carries a Price, Durasteel column giving that part's finished cost outright -- ceil(Volume × Density × CR/lb × 3), the ×3 being Lightsaber Construction (IQ/Hard), already marked up. Add the printed figures together; do not re-derive them from volume, and do not pool raw values and round once at the end. For a part milled from any other material, scale from its own density and CR/lb by the same formula. Printing the per-component figures removes the rounding slack that an unstated order leaves behind: two people adding the same four numbers now get the same answer, and any catalogued weapon's Base Cost is checkable by addition alone.

Name every component. A catalogued weapon must list one specific part in each slot, never a choice -- “any Very Common crystal” gives no Base Cost anyone can check, and an entry nothing can check is an entry that stays wrong. Where a build is a unique showcase rather than a purchasable pattern, say so and mark its price as set rather than derived, so a reader knows the figure is the GM's and not the formula's.

Constructing a Lightsaber

When a Force-user wishes to construct a custom lightsaber from scratch—following the structural path of the bottom-up modular system—the process is a sacred, meditative exercise. It requires aligning the internal geometry, hardwiring the electronics, and sealing the chassis in strict chronological order: Chassis Hardware > Internal Components > Attunement Crystal.

Lightsaber Assembly -- the Exception: Constructing a lightsaber from its parts needs no Blueprint. A character with Lightsaber Construction (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}) is trained to build lightsabers -- Jedi and Sith raise their own as a rite -- and that training is the plan. It covers assembly only: the component parts, when the character manufactures them, are not exempt. Handgrip components (Crafting Handgrip Components, above) and internal modules (Crafting Internal Components, above) are each ordinary builds that need their own Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}), bought or reverse-engineered. Buy the parts and a trained hand assembles the saber freely; mill them yourself and each milled part wants its plan.

Each phase of construction requires specific skill checks to ensure structural integrity and functional energy containment.

Assembly Sequence

Phase 1: Handgrip Assembly

Before any energy matrices or crystals can be integrated, the physical hilt components—the Emitter, Switch, Sleeve, and Pommel/Coupler—must be forged or acquired and securely joined together to form the weapon’s physical housing.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check based on the final weight distribution and threading of the hilt parts.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The hilt components join seamlessly, ensuring perfect balance, proper weight distribution, and a secure structural seal.
  • Standard Failure: The hilt is misaligned or the casing is improperly sealed. 50% of the raw materials (or the value of the hilt parts) are wasted and must be replaced before attempting assembly again.
  • Critical Failure: The metal warps, threads strip catastrophically, or structural stress ruins 100% of the hilt materials, forcing the crafter to start completely over with fresh components.

Phase 2: Internal Integration

With the physical hilt assembled and hollowed, the internal modules—the Power Cell, Lens Assembly, and Emitter Matrix, alongside any optional Secondary Power Crystals—must be installed and hardwired into the chassis.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. Builders without points in this skill may still attempt the roll at its default (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}), but forfeit any Force-attunement bonuses provided later.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check for the internal module block and wiring array.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The delicate wiring is soldered cleanly, lenses align, and power cells seat properly into the chassis matrix without resistance.
  • Standard Failure: The delicate wiring fuses or the clari-crystalline lens is misaligned. No physical materials are wasted, but the power matrix fails to sync. The crafter must spend 1 additional hour of meticulous rewiring and attempt a new roll.
  • Critical Failure: The emitter matrix or power cell violently shorts out during testing. All base internal materials are destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy damage from the sudden electrical and plasma surge.

Phase 3: Crystal Attunement

The final step of construction is seating the Primary Focusing (Kyber) Crystal. This is the heart of the weapon, requiring the builder to use the Force to perfectly align the crystal’s microscopic lattice with the established plasma stream and internal matrix.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. (Builders without points in this skill may still attempt the roll at its default (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}), but forfeit any Force-attunement bonuses provided by the crystal.)
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check during a dedicated hour of deep meditation and calibration.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The crystal resonates harmoniously with the matrix. The lightsaber hums to life, stabilizing its blade perfectly and unlocking all baseline stats and crystal bonuses.
  • Standard Failure: The mystical link fails to lock. The physical weapon is entirely intact, but the energy matrix misaligns, preventing the blade from igniting. No materials are lost, but the crafter must spend 1 additional hour in deep meditation to realign the crystal before making a new roll.
  • Critical Failure: A disastrous attunement failure introduces a hidden structural and energetic flaw. The weapon appears to function normally during diagnostic checks, but will suffer a catastrophic power overload on its very first strike—inflicting 3d energy damage directly to the user’s hand and completely destroying all internal components.

Disassembly

When a Force-user wishes to gracefully dismantle a lightsaber—whether to swap a component, upgrade a crystal, or retire the weapon—the process is treated as a structured, meditative reversal of the assembly steps. Unlike rushed field stripping, this technique relies on the Force and precise internal manipulation.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Disassembly can likewise record a Blueprint of the hilt (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- the hardware phases only. Crystal Attunement is personal, and can never be recorded.

Each phase of disassembly requires specific checks to safely separate the layers.

Disassembly Sequence

To completely take down a lightsaber via meditation, the crafter must work in a strict reverse order of assembly: Attunement Crystal > Internal Components > Chassis Hardware.

Phase 1: Removing the Primary Focusing (Kyber) Crystal

Because the primary crystal is the energetic heart of the weapon, it must be unseated first while the containment field remains stable.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. (Builders without points may still attempt the roll at its default (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}).)
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The crystal is unseated flawlessly. It retains 100% of its value and any Force-attunement bonuses.
  • Standard Failure: The attunement link resists. The process takes twice as long, but the crystal is unharmed.
  • Critical Failure: The crafter loses focus or misaligns the magnetic seals. The crystal suffers micro-fractures (imparting a permanent -1 penalty to attack rolls if reused), and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy damage from a minor containment backflow.

Phase 2: Extracting Internal Components

Once the crystal is clear, the internal electronics—the Power Cell, Lens Assembly, and Emitter Matrix—must be disconnected from the chassis hardwiring.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. (Builders without points may still attempt the roll at its default (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}).)
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check for the internal module block.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: All internal components slide free completely undamaged and fully reusable.
  • Standard Failure: The delicate wiring fuses or micro-soldering warps. The internal components are safely extracted but ruined as junk (yielding standard salvage raw material weight).
  • Critical Failure: A power surge shorts out the matrix. The internals are entirely destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy damage from a localized plasma discharge.

Phase 3: Unsealing and Dismantling Chassis Hardware

With the interior entirely hollowed out, the outer hilt pieces—the Emitter, Switch, Sleeve, and Pommel/Coupler—can be unscrewed and separated.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The hilt components unseal smoothly, yielding 100% reusable hardware and raw metals.
  • Standard Failure: Threading seizes up due to plasma residue, requiring twice the base time to wrench apart. Parts remain intact.
  • Critical Failure: The chassis warps or a hidden trap mechanism (if built with a Trapped Switch) triggers unexpectedly, ruining the hilt parts and forcing defense rolls against the trap’s specified damage.

Component Swapping

When a Force-user or technician needs to swap specific modular parts—such as exchanging an Emitter, swapping out a internal Lens, or replacing a Power Cell—without performing a full, ground-up rebuild of the weapon, they use the Component Swapping rules.

Time Required

  • Base Swap Time: 50% of the total time required for a complete disassembly and re-assembly sequence.
  • Multiple Component Modifier: Add +5 minutes to the total swap time for every part swapped after the first item in the same operation.

Example: If a full meditative take-down and re-assembly takes 2 hours (120 minutes) total, swapping a single part takes 60 minutes. Swapping three parts simultaneously takes 70 minutes (60-minute base + 10 minutes for two extra parts).

Component Swapping Sequence & Checks

Swapping parts requires making specific skill checks depending on which layer of the weapon is being opened and modified. All components being installed must already be fully fabricated or acquired beforehand.

Step 1: Outer Chassis Swapping (Hardware)

Applies when replacing physical hilt parts (Emitter, Switch, Sleeve, or Pommel/Coupler).

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check to unthread, replace, and realign the outer physical housing.
  • Critical Success / Success: The new hilt component seals flawlessly into the housing, aligning with internal power feeds without damaging the structural threading.
  • Standard Failure: The threading seizes or misaligns. The swap fails and takes twice as long. No parts are destroyed, but the weapon cannot ignite until a successful swap roll is made.
  • Critical Failure: Casing stress or stripped threading ruins the newly attempted component, rendering it useless as scrap.

Step 2: Internal Module Swapping (Electronics & Optics)

Applies when replacing internal components (Power Cell, Lens Assembly, or Emitter Matrix).

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check to unhook delicate micro-soldering, pull the old module, and integrate the replacement into the internal power block.
  • Critical Success / Success: Wiring, lens casing, and power channels sync seamlessly into the chassis matrix.
  • Standard Failure: The internal wiring fuses or optic geometry misaligns. The swap fails, requiring 1 additional hour of troubleshooting before re-attempting the roll.
  • Critical Failure: A short circuit occurs during testing. The replacement module is completely destroyed, and the crafter takes 1d-3 energy damage from an electrical surge.

Step 3: Crystal Swap & Re-Attunement

Applies when swapping the Primary Focusing (Kyber) Crystal or Secondary Power Crystals.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. (Builders without points may still attempt the roll at its default (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}), but forfeit all Force-attunement bonuses.)
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check during the final phase of the swap to align the new crystal with the plasma stream.
  • Critical Success / Success: The new crystal locks into the matrix, instantly stabilizing the blade and granting all baseline stats and special traits.
  • Standard Failure: The Force resonance fails to lock. The weapon cannot ignite. The crafter must spend 1 hour in deep meditation to realign the crystal before rolling again.
  • Critical Failure: Hidden matrix flaw. The weapon appears functional, but overloads on its first strike—inflicting 3d energy damage to the user’s hand and destroying all internal modules.

Salvaging

If a lightsaber is captured, badly damaged in combat, or being torn apart by someone rushing the job or lacking the esoteric knowledge of Lightsaber Construction, standard salvaging rules apply. In these scenarios, the salvager is actively fighting the weapon’s sealed chassis and micro-soldered internals.

Because the weapon is modular, a salvager can choose to target Specific Intact Components (e.g., trying to save the Dual-Phase Emitter or the Corusca Gem Power Cell) or simply strip the hilt for Raw Material Weight (e.g., melting down a Curved Sleeve for its Electrum weight).

Salvaging Sequence

To successfully break down a lightsaber under salvage conditions, the process is handled in structured phases. Note: If dealing with a Trapped Switch, the salvager must first successfully roll against Traps to identify and bypass the security measure before attempting physical salvage.

Phase 1: Breaching the Chassis

The salvager must force open or bypass any outer casing locks, seals, or traps to access the inner core.

  • Skill Check Required:
  • For Chassis/Hardware: Lightsaber Construction. A salvager without it may use Armoury (Melee Weapons) at a -4 penalty, or Machinist at full skill -- breaching a chassis is forcing metal, and a machinist does that for a living. Machinist is a full-skill route for this phase only; it does not reach Phase 2 or Phase 3, where the work is electronics and containment. (Scrounging may be used at a -5 penalty if the goal is only to recover raw scrap metal).
  • If Trapped: Traps skill check first.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The outer hilt unseals or is breached cleanly without damaging the internal stacking.
  • Standard Failure: The casing warps or jams, increasing the time required to break into the core.
  • Critical Failure: The chassis warps violently, or (if not bypassed) a hidden Trapped Switch triggers unexpectedly, forcing defense rolls against the trap’s specified damage and ruining the outer hardware.

Phase 2: Stripping the Internal Module Block

Once the housing is open, the salvager attempts to extract the fragile electronics—the Power Cell, Lens Assembly, and Emitter Matrix.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. Without it, Armoury (Melee Weapons) or Electronics Repair (Powered Melee) at a -4 penalty, or Scrounging at -5, due to the microscopic fragility of the parts.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check for the internal module block.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The internal components are freed intact (preserving targeted components depending on overall success tier).
  • Standard Failure: The component shatters, fuses, or shorts out completely during extraction. Yield is ruined.
  • Critical Failure: The residual energy in the power cell or emitter matrix violently discharges. All internal modules are destroyed, and the salvager takes 1d-3 energy damage (minimum 1) from the plasma burst.

Phase 3: Securing the Primary Focusing (Kyber) Crystal

The final step of salvage is extracting the primary crystal from the collapsing containment matrix.

  • Skill Check Required: Lightsaber Construction. Without it, Armoury (Melee Weapons) or Electronics Repair (Powered Melee) at a -4 penalty, or Scrounging at -5.
  • The Roll: Make a single skill check.
  • Outcomes:
  • Critical Success / Success: The crystal is safely extracted unblemished.
  • Standard Failure: The rough extraction introduces micro-fractures; if reused, the crystal now imparts a permanent -1 penalty to attack rolls.
  • Critical Failure: The containment field collapses entirely. The crystal is completely pulverized, yielding zero salvage value.

Overall Salvage Yield Outcomes

When attempting a salvage operation, the player must declare whether they are trying to extract a specific component intact or just stripping it for raw material wealth, and then evaluate the final result of their skill rolls:

  • Critical Success:
  • If targeting components: You successfully extract the Primary Kyber Crystal, plus you perfectly preserve two additional reusable modular components of your choice (e.g., a Shoto Sleeve and a Firkrann Lens). All other parts are reduced to 75% of their raw material weight.
  • If scrapping for materials: You recover 75% of the total raw material weight of the hilt (metals, wiring, gems) and successfully extract the Primary Focusing Crystal safely.
  • Standard Success:
  • If targeting components: You successfully extract the Primary Kyber Crystal, plus one additional reusable modular component of your choice. All other internal upgrades and hardware are ruined, yielding only 50% of their base material weight in scrap.
  • If scrapping for materials: Recovers 50% of the original material weight (hilt metals, wiring) and safely extracts the Primary Focusing Crystal. Other internal upgrades are ruined.
  • Standard Failure: The weapon is clumsily stripped. The hilt is crushed or warped, and the delicate lenses, matrices, and power cells are shattered. The weapon is reduced to useless junk, yielding no recoverable materials except a potentially flawed Primary Crystal (which now imparts a -1 penalty to attack rolls if ever reused).
  • Critical Failure: Disaster. The power cell punctures or the magnetic containment field violently collapses during the forced disassembly. All materials, components, and crystals are completely destroyed. The salvager takes 1d-3 energy damage (minimum 1) from the resulting plasma discharge. (If the hilt had an active Trapped Switch that was not bypassed, trigger the trap’s specific damage instead).
